author: high
claim: Subgoal existence is solved directly: a simultaneous solution is obtained from Bézout selector integers.
evidence:
First prove Bézout's identity for the only pairs used. If A,B are coprime positive integers, let c be the least positive integer of the form rA+sB. Division of A by c leaves a remainder which is also an integer linear combination of A,B; minimality forces that remainder to be 0. The same holds for B. Hence c divides both A and B, so c=1.

For fixed i, put M_i=the product of m_j over j!=i (the empty product is 1). For each j!=i, pairwise coprimeness and Bézout give p_ij m_j+q_ij m_i=1. Multiply these identities over all j!=i. In the expansion, the term choosing p_ij m_j from every factor is U_i M_i, where U_i is the product of p_ij, and every other term is divisible by m_i. Thus 1=U_i M_i+V_i m_i for some integer V_i. Set e_i=U_i M_i. Then e_i is 1 modulo m_i, while for r!=i the factor m_r occurs in M_i, so e_i is 0 modulo m_r. Therefore x=sum_i a_i e_i satisfies x congruent to a_r modulo m_r for every r.

links.subgoal: Existence of x satisfying every congruence
links.attempt_summary: Construct orthogonal congruence selectors by multiplying pairwise Bézout identities.

glossary.M_i: the product of all moduli except m_i
glossary.p_ij: the coefficient of m_j in a pairwise Bézout identity
glossary.q_ij: the coefficient of m_i in a pairwise Bézout identity
glossary.U_i: the product of p_ij over j different from i
glossary.V_i: the remaining integer coefficient of m_i after expansion
glossary.c: the least positive linear combination in the proof of Bézout's identity
glossary.r: an index or an integer coefficient as specified by context
glossary.s: an integer coefficient in Bézout's identity

author: high
claim: Subgoal uniqueness is solved directly: any common multiple of the pairwise coprime moduli is divisible by their product.
evidence: Let x and y both satisfy all the congruences and put d=x-y. Then m_i divides d for every i. We prove by induction that P_r=m_1...m_r divides d. This is immediate for r=1. Suppose P_r divides d and write d=P_r q. For each j<=r, pairwise coprimeness and Bézout give alpha_j m_j+beta_j m_{r+1}=1. Multiplying all r identities and collecting the unique term containing all alpha_j m_j gives 1=A P_r+B m_{r+1} for some integers A,B. Multiply by q: q=A d+B m_{r+1}q. Since m_{r+1} divides d, both terms on the right are divisible by m_{r+1}; hence m_{r+1} divides q. Therefore P_{r+1} divides d. At r=k this says M divides x-y, exactly x congruent to y modulo M.

links.attempt_summary: Inductively multiply each new pairwise coprime modulus into a divisor of x-y.

glossary.P_r: the partial product m_1 times through m_r
glossary.alpha_j: the coefficient of m_j in a pairwise Bézout identity
glossary.beta_j: the coefficient of m_{r+1} in a pairwise Bézout identity

author: high
claim:
Let \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\) be pairwise coprime integers greater than \(1\), and let \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) be arbitrary integers. Prove that there is an integer \(x\) satisfying
\[
x\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i}\qquad(1\le i\le k),
\]
and that any two such integers are congruent modulo \(M=m_1m_2\cdots m_k\).
evidence:
Assume \(k\ge 1\). We first prove the form of Bézout's identity that will be used twice. Let \(A,B\) be coprime positive integers. The set
\[
S=\{rA+sB:r,s\in\mathbb Z,\ rA+sB>0\}
\]
is nonempty because \(A\in S\). By the well-ordering principle, let \(c\) be its least element, so \(c=r_0A+s_0B\) for some \(r_0,s_0\in\mathbb Z\). By the division algorithm, write \(A=qc+t\), where \(q,t\in\mathbb Z\) and \(0\le t<c\). Then
\[
t=A-qc=(1-qr_0)A-qs_0B.
\]
If \(t>0\), then \(t\in S\), contradicting the minimality of \(c\). Hence \(t=0\), so \(c\mid A\). Applying the same argument after dividing \(B\) by \(c\) shows \(c\mid B\). Since \(A\) and \(B\) are coprime and \(c>0\), it follows that \(c=1\). Consequently there exist integers \(r,s\) such that \(rA+sB=1\).

For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), define
\[
M_i=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le k\\j\ne i}}m_j,
\]
with an empty product equal to \(1\). For every \(j\ne i\), pairwise coprimeness gives \(\gcd(m_j,m_i)=1\). By the proved Bézout identity, choose integers \(b_{ij},c_{ij}\) such that
\[
b_{ij}m_j+c_{ij}m_i=1.
\]
Multiplying these identities over all \(j\ne i\), and using the empty-product convention when \(k=1\), gives
\[
1=\prod_{j\ne i}(b_{ij}m_j+c_{ij}m_i)=u_iM_i+v_im_i
\]
for some integers \(u_i,v_i\). Indeed, the term obtained by selecting \(b_{ij}m_j\) from every factor is
\[
\left(\prod_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\right)M_i=u_iM_i,
\]
and every other term in the expansion contains at least one factor \(m_i\), so the sum of all those other terms is \(v_im_i\). For \(k=1\), take \(u_1=1\) and \(v_1=0\).

Set \(e_i=u_iM_i\) and define the integer
\[
x_0=\sum_{i=1}^k a_ie_i.
\]
Fix \(r\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). The identity \(1=u_rM_r+v_rm_r\) shows that \(e_r\equiv1\pmod{m_r}\). If \(i\ne r\), then \(m_r\) is one of the factors of \(M_i\), so \(m_r\mid e_i\) and \(e_i\equiv0\pmod{m_r}\). Therefore
\[
x_0-a_r=a_r(e_r-1)+\sum_{\substack{1\le i\le k\\i\ne r}}a_ie_i
\]
is divisible by \(m_r\). Thus \(x_0\equiv a_r\pmod{m_r}\). Since \(r\) was arbitrary, \(x_0\) satisfies all the required congruences, proving existence.

It remains to prove uniqueness modulo the full product. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be any two integers satisfying all the required congruences, and put \(d=x-y\). For each \(i\), both \(x\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i}\) and \(y\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i}\), so \(m_i\mid d\).

For \(1\le r\le k\), put \(P_r=m_1m_2\cdots m_r\). We prove by induction on \(r\) that \(P_r\mid d\). The assertion for \(r=1\) is \(m_1\mid d\), already proved. Suppose \(1\le r<k\) and \(P_r\mid d\). Write \(d=P_rq\) with \(q\in\mathbb Z\). For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), the integers \(m_j\) and \(m_{r+1}\) are coprime, so choose integers \(\alpha_j,\beta_j\) satisfying
\[
\alpha_jm_j+\beta_jm_{r+1}=1.
\]
Multiplying these \(r\) identities gives
\[
1=\prod_{j=1}^r(\alpha_jm_j+\beta_jm_{r+1})
  =A_rP_r+B_rm_{r+1}
\]
for some integers \(A_r,B_r\): the term choosing \(\alpha_jm_j\) from every factor is \(A_rP_r\), where \(A_r=\prod_{j=1}^r\alpha_j\), and every other term contains the factor \(m_{r+1}\). Multiplying this identity by \(q\) yields
\[
q=A_rP_rq+B_rm_{r+1}q=A_rd+B_rm_{r+1}q.
\]
The first term on the right is divisible by \(m_{r+1}\) because \(m_{r+1}\mid d\), and the second term is divisible by \(m_{r+1}\) by its displayed form. Hence \(m_{r+1}\mid q\). Thus \(P_{r+1}=P_rm_{r+1}\mid d\), completing the induction.

Taking \(r=k\), we obtain \(M=P_k\mid d=x-y\). Therefore \(x\equiv y\pmod M\), so any two solutions are congruent modulo \(M\), as required.

links.attempt_summary: Self-contained Bézout-selector proof of existence and product-divisibility induction for uniqueness.

glossary.k: a positive integer giving the number of congruences
glossary.M: the product m_1 m_2 through m_k
glossary.M_i: the product of all m_j with j different from i
glossary.u_i: the coefficient making u_i M_i congruent to 1 modulo m_i
glossary.v_i: the companion coefficient in u_i M_i+v_i m_i=1
glossary.d: the difference x-y of two simultaneous solutions
glossary.P_r: the partial product m_1 m_2 through m_r
glossary.A_r: the coefficient of P_r in a Bézout identity with m_{r+1}
glossary.B_r: the coefficient of m_{r+1} in that identity
